In the meantime, Vietnam’s foreign policy attaches importance to promoting relationships with “major powers and important partners.” Obviously, Vietnam sees Canada as “an important partner.”
Taken together, these three reasons converge on a single conclusion: among Vietnam’s plausible next upgrades, Canada is the most logical choice.
Indeed, what makes this more than a hypothesis is that Hanoi and Ottawa are visibly moving in this direction already. In January 2026, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a widely noted address describing a “rupture” in the rules-based international order and calling on middle powers to cooperate more closely to protect their interests as great-power rivalry intensifies. On the Vietnamese side, the signals have been just as direct. On June 29, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung told Canada’s ambassador that Hanoi “always regards Canada as an important partner” and pressed for expanded cooperation in trade, artificial intelligence, quantum technology and semiconductors. Hung also told the guest that Vietnam “wishes to elevate ties with Canada to a new level.”  In the meantime, Vietnam’s National Assembly Chairman voiced confidence that the two sides would bring their partnership “to new heights.”
Most recently, on August 22, Vietnam’s Foreign Minister asked his Canadian counterpart “to work closely to materialize the upgrade of ties as anticipated by leaders of both sides.” The Canadian Foreign Minister responded positively. Both capitals are actively laying groundwork for an upgrade.
The upgrade of ties is not a one-way wish. In fact, the logic runs both ways. Canada is a developed, technologically advanced economy that can support Vietnam’s ambitious “centennial” development goals – Hanoi’s targets, tied to the 2030 and 2045 anniversaries of the Communist Party and the state, for becoming a high-income, technology-driven nation. Canadian officials have flagged priority cooperation areas including AI, semiconductors, nuclear energy, aerospace, and high-quality workforce training – precisely the sectors Vietnam needs to climb the value chain.

articles.title: Indonesia, United States Kick Off Annual Multinational Military Exercises
articles.full_text:
Super Garuda Shield 2026 will involve more than 4,700 troops from 13 nations, and observers from a further eight others.
U.S., Indonesian, and South Korean marines, as well as personnel from the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force, stand at attention during an opening ceremony for Exercise Super Garuda Shield 26 at the Indonesian Marine Corps 7th Infantry Battalion base near Lampung, Indonesia, Aug. 31, 2026.
The United States and Indonesia launched annual multilateral military exercises yesterday, which the two sides said aimed to improve interoperability and bolster deterrence in the region.
Super Garuda Shield, which has been held annually since 2007, will take place in various locations including Bandung, Lampung, Kalimantan, and the Indonesian Army’s Baturaja Combat Training Center in South Sumatra before concluding in Jakarta on September 11.
This year’s iteration will involve more than 4,743 personnel from 13 other countries including Japan, ​South Korea, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. A further eight nations will join as observers. While the total number of troops is slightly down on last year’s iteration, which featured a record 5,400 participants, it includes more participating nations than ever, with India taking part as an observer for the first time.
Major General Patrick Ellis, the commanding general of the U.S. Army’s 4th Infantry Division, said that the exercise was critical for “building the human architecture that keeps the Indo-Pacific safe.”
“The security landscape of the Indo-Pacific is complex and readiness cannot be surged when a crisis begins,” he said at an opening ceremony at the Indonesian Armed Forces’ School of Command in Bandung. He added, “We are not just meeting for another annual training cycle. We are writing a historic new chapter in our ​bilateral relationship.”
TNI Commander General Agus Subiyanto, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, said that “the purpose of the exercise is, first, diplomacy, and then cooperation through the exchange of capabilities.”
The Garuda Shield exercise was established between the U.S. and Indonesian militaries in 2007 and forms a primary pillar of the two nations’ defense relationship. “Super” was added to its title in 2022, when the exercise was expanded into a multilateral format.
This year, the exercises “will include a joint staff exercise, cyber exercise, airborne operations, jungle training, and amphibious exercise,” the U.S. Army said in a statement.  U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard personnel will also conduct coordinated maritime training serials with the Indonesian Navy in adjacent waters in order “to strengthen joint interoperability at sea.”
Participating forces will also take part in special forces infiltration drills, cyber defense exercises, the firing of Stinger missiles, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations.
The expanded exercise is the first to take place since Indonesia and the U.S. established a new defense cooperation pact in April. The Major Defense Cooperation Partnership (MDCP) will bolster cooperation in Indonesian military modernization and increase training, joint exercises, and professional military education, with the aim of “maintaining peace and stability” in Asia.
Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said at the time that they “have also committed to enhance joint special forces training,” and to expand existing multilateral exercises, including Super Garuda Shield.
The continued expansion of the annual exercise speaks to the continued good health of the U.S.-Indonesia defense partnership, which has remained stable despite the erratic nature of foreign policymaking under the second Trump administration. However, while Indonesia has welcomed closer U.S. security cooperation, it continues to hew to a policy of foreign policy non-alignment, and to maintain a balanced spread of defense engagements – including with key U.S. adversaries.
For example, on the same day that Sjafrie and Hegseth signed the MDCP agreement in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto was being hosted at the Kremlin by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
And last month, Indonesia agreed to boost its military ties with China during a visit to Jakarta by the country’s foreign and ​defense ministers. The two sides agreed to increase joint exercises and officer exchanges. They also discussed the establishment of a joint munitions factory in Indonesia that would include a possible transfer of technology from China. Also in August, Jakarta courted controversy when an Indonesian frigate conducted a joint navigation exercise with China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy in the waters east of Taiwan – the first time that China had exercised with a foreign military in the area.
Later this year, China and Indonesia are scheduled to hold their Heping Garuda joint military exercises, which took place for the first time in December 2024. These much narrower drills will focus mostly on humanitarian aid and disaster relief operations.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing to Visit Vietnam Soon, State Media Says
articles.full_text:
All four mainland Southeast Asian states have now extended an official invitation to the general-turned-president since his inauguration in April.
Myanmar’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, will soon visit Vietnam, his fourth visit to an ASEAN member state since taking office in April, Myanmar state media reported today.
According to a report in the Global New Light of Myanmar, the former general will travel to Vietnam “in the near future” at the invitation of To Lam, Vietnam’s president and the head of the Communist Party of Vietnam. In addition to meeting with Lam, he will also meet with Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh and Tran Thanh Man, the head of the National Assembly, and “receive representatives from economic organizations.”
“During the visit, the President will hold cordial discussions and exchange views on further consolidation of the existing friendly relations…  as well as cooperation across economic, cultural, and various other sectors,” the report stated.
The announcement, which has not yet been confirmed by Hanoi, comes shortly after Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung traveled to Myanmar last week, the first time that a Vietnamese foreign minister has visited the country since the 2021 coup. During talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw, he “discussed boosting bilateral trade and investment, as well as mutual support on the international stage,” The Irrawaddy reported, citing state media.
Trung also met Lower House speaker Khin Yi and Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, to whom he pledged “continued support for Myanmar at the U.N., ASEAN, and other international forums.” Trung also reportedly extended a formal invitation for Min Aung Hlaing to visit Hanoi.
The trip would be the former general’s fourth to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since taking office as president in April, after visits to Laos in early July and Thailand last month and an upcoming trip to Cambodia in early September. He has also made state visits to India and China in June, and to Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan last month.
All of this reflects a concerted push by Min Aung Hlaing to consolidate Myanmar’s relationship with key partners. A top priority, which he mentioned in his inauguration speech in April, is to normalize relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Since late 2021, the 11-nation bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government, which was formed after flawed multi-phase elections in December and January, has taken an increasingly defiant line toward ASEAN, dismissing the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted “interference” in its internal affairs and demanding its full readmission to the bloc.
At the same time, it has sought to engage directly with willing ASEAN member states, particularly Thailand, which has positioned itself as a bridge between Myanmar and ASEAN. During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Bangkok last month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul “reaffirmed” Thailand’s commitment “to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.”
The fact that all four of Myanmar’s mainland Southeast Asian neighbors have now extended invitations to Min Aung Hlaing to visit reflects a growing regional fatigue with the Myanmar conflict, and a belief that “calibrated reengagement” (in Thailand’s phrase) is the best way to manage the effects of the civil war, if not to resolve it.
It also reflects a continuing divergence between ASEAN’s mainland and maritime member states on how to deal with Myanmar. Over the past five years, the mainland states have favored more engagement than maritime nations such as Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia, which have advocated a more robust regional response to the military coup in Myanmar. Whether and to what extent Myanmar manages to make inroads into this camp, which is reportedly also growing with the protracted deadlock inside Myanmar, may become clear in the run-up to the next ASEAN summit in November.

articles.title: The ‘Unique’ Communications That Saved Lives Before Nepal’s Devastating Flood
articles.full_text:
Survivors and experts say that instant word-of-mouth warnings may have saved hundreds of lives on August 26.
A view of Langtang Lirung, a mountain in Langtang National Park, Nepal, from the southeast. A glacier collapse on the north face of the mountain is believed to be the proximate cause of the devastating flash floods on August 26, 2026.
Families and experts in Nepal have told of the devastating flood that killed over 900 and the little-known cultural phenomenon that may have saved even more lives from being lost.
According to those on the ground, while the waters surged through villages and left over 4,200 missing around the border between Nepal and China, some families had advanced warning of the imminent disaster.
“In Nepal, people-to-people information sharing is quite good and also a unique phenomenon,” Dr Basanta Raj Adhikari, the director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at the Institute of Engineering at Tribhuvan University in Kirtipur, Kathmandu, told The Diplomat.
According to Adhikari, in times of an environmental disaster such as an earthquake, landslide, or flood such as the one witnessed on August 26, news travels fast, with villages higher up in the mountains quickly passing information to those in the lower lands, and warning residents that danger is on the way.
“People upstream give information to those lower down so that they can save themselves,” Basanta said.
This informal method of sounding the alarm appears to have worked for some families along the Trishuli River where the flood waters arose. These included Rita Tamang, who lives in Daring, Gajuri, along the Prithvi Highway which sits beside the waterway.
“Before the flood came, we had moved a little higher up from our house, but we still witnessed the flood very clearly. It was absolutely terrifying. The flood was not just carrying a huge amount of water; it was also sweeping away all kinds of things, causing massive destruction. Our house was also badly damaged, with almost half of it destroyed,” the 34-year-old housewife told The Diplomat.
“We knew about the flood coming from Rasuwagadhi about two to four hours beforehand. But we had never seen a flood this severe and terrifying before. In fact, we had never witnessed anything like this in our lives.”
Tamang said that the flood completely washed away three concrete bridges that vehicles used to cross the river, and destroyed a key suspension bridge in the area.
It was Tamang’s brother, 32-year-old Bikram Tamang, who helped to save her life.
Bikram Tamang said that he had been at the China-Nepal border working as a truck driver and transporting goods from the border to Kathmandu, Birgunj, Pokhara, and other cities in Nepal.
After delivering the goods, drivers usually return with empty trucks, Tamang said, and Bikram had just dropped off a delivery when he got news of a torrent of water approaching.
“His friends informed him that a dam had apparently burst and that a massive flood had come. They told everyone to stay safe and not to go near the riverbank,” she said. “From there, my brother directly called us at home, and that is how we came to know about the flood.”
It is thought that the Nepal flood wave was caused by a glacial collapse after a large chunk of ice from a glacier broke off and fell into a river. This ice then melted, mixing with river water and debris, before gushing through mountain gulleys and destroying villages, towns, bridges, roads, and homes.
As a result of the advanced warning from her younger sibling, Tamang and her family were able to scramble to higher ground.
Both Basanta and Tamang said that, in times of disaster, word-of-mouth was often faster than official warnings, although Tamang explained that both Ncell and Namaste, two major telecommunications networks in Nepal, had managed to send alerts to their subscribers that a major flood had occurred.
The alerts also advised residents to evacuate areas along the Trishuli River.
However, both Basanta and Tamang said that time was of the essence when a disaster occurred as both internet and phone signals were disrupted once power lines were destroyed.
Basanta added that the risk of secondary flooding from lakes swelling upstream and bursting was an ongoing threat, and that it would be a consideration for search and rescue teams looking for survivors and the deceased. However, the information and people-to-people sharing that was used when the first flood happened would likely be harnessed again by those working in the area.
“The Nepal government is aware of the risks and is working closely to get information from those upstream to those lower down,” Dr Basanta said.
He explained that there would be a similar chain of information sharing by the local authorities, using other devices such as satellite phones or walkie-talkies, that would allow those working on higher ground to warn if more floods were coming, in the event that normal phone lines and internet were still disrupted.
Following the first wave, the fear that more floods would follow came to fruition for Tamang, who said that many families were choosing to sleep outside their homes in case rising waters caused buildings to wash away completely.
“On Sunday, the flood came again at around five in the morning and, on Saturday, a very large flood came from the stream near our village which forced many families to leave their homes,” she said.
She added that they were safe for now but that, with every new wave of water, the family had to move to higher ground and wait for it to subside before returning to their partially damaged home.
“People are in a very difficult situation. Most of their belongings are outside and they have nowhere safe to stay. There are children, elderly people, parents, and people with disabilities among them.”
And while Tamang’s brother Bikram was initially able to make contact and urge his family to seek shelter, communication has now completely ceased, even though internet and phone connections have been restored in her area.
“As far as we know, he was in contact with his family until he had loaded his vehicle inside the Chinese border area and was about to leave. There has been no information about his whereabouts or condition,” Tamang said.
“We don’t know whether he is alive, safe, or what has happened to him. We have tried repeatedly to contact him, but his mobile phone is completely unreachable.”
articles.summary: Survivors and experts say that instant word-of-mouth warnings may have saved hundreds of lives on August 26.

articles.title: How Great Power Rivalry Is Fracturing the Pacific Islands Forum
articles.full_text:
Absences from this year’s Leaders’ Meeting are raising questions about the group’s solidarity amid growing China-U.S. competition.
The Smaller Island States (SIS) Leaders Meeting kicks off the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting week in Palau, Aug. 31, 2026.
The 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders’ Meeting opened on August 31 under a banner of unity, but it can’t escape the reality that outside powers are competing for influence in the Pacific. The question now facing the PIF is whether the forum’s consensus model, once a safeguard for small-state sovereignty, has become the very mechanism through which that influence reshapes regional outcomes.
The official theme of this year’s PIF Leaders’ Meeting, held in Palau, is B.E.L.A.U., or Building Economies, Life, Action, Unity, an acronym that doubles as a tribute to the host nation’s indigenous name. It was meant to signal collective resolve. Instead, the gathering has been defined by conspicuous absences and blocked consensus. Given the return of Taiwan as a development partner after last year’s exclusion, some see this year’s PIF as proof of Beijing’s growing capacity to paralyze the region’s most important multilateral institution from within.
At least five Pacific leaders chose not to attend. The leaders of Kiribati, Samoa, and Vanuatu dispatched deputies, while Fiji’s Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka stayed home to manage domestic affairs. The most dramatic absence was that of Solomon Islands’ Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who landed in Palau only to leave hours later after a no-confidence motion was filed against him back in Honiara. Wale had served as prime minister for barely three months and as outgoing PIF chair, was meant to hand the gavel to Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr. Instead, he left Foreign Minister Rick Hou to represent his country at the summit.
Kiribati’s case is particularly revealing. President Taneti Maamau dispatched not a cabinet minister but David Teaabo, his director of foreign service and a former ambassador to China. In an organization where decisions require consensus at the level of heads of state, sending a lower-ranking delegate who cannot commit to communique language with full authority is itself a political statement.
Kiribati’s posture becomes clearer against the backdrop of the missile crisis that preceded the summit. On July 6, China conducted a submarine-launched ballistic missile test in the Pacific, firing what Taiwan identified as a JL-2 from the South China Sea. The missile, carrying a dummy warhead, transited the exclusive economic zones of the Federated States of Micronesia, Naoero (formerly Nauru), and Kiribati before landing near Tuvalu’s maritime boundary. Beijing provided only a few hours’ notice to the affected Pacific Island nations.
The reaction was swift – at least from those countries that did respond. Papua New Guinea’s Prime Minister James Marape invoked the region’s traumatic history of nuclear testing, insisting that Pacific nations “do not want history repeated.” Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the test “provocative” and “destabilizing.” Yet when Pacific foreign ministers gathered in Fiji in early August, Kiribati and Naoero blocked the consensus needed to issue a joint condemnation.
The PIF has historically operated on the principle of unanimity, a practice rooted in what Pacific leaders call the “Pacific Way,” designed to ensure that no island nation, however small, could be overruled by its larger neighbors. But the model assumed that external pressures would remain at the margins of PIF deliberations. When a member state with deep ties to the power responsible for a security event deploys its consensus rights to shield that power from collective criticism, the model risks becoming a means of undermining collective action.
New Zealand’s Foreign Minister Winston Peters made the frustration explicit, noting that two countries “were seeking to use the need for consensus as a veto provision.” Peters said that he had “made it very clear that we didn’t think outsiders should be telling insiders” what positions to take.
Kiribati’s alignment with Beijing extends beyond the blocking of a PIF statement. In late August, its parliament passed the first reading of a constitutional amendment that would restrict diplomatic recognition to states holding U.N. membership or permanent observer status, effectively locking future governments into recognizing Beijing. Graeme Smith of the Australian National University characterized the move as “almost entirely about sending a message to Beijing.”
With that in mind, Taiwan’s return to the PIF may also have contributed to Kiribati’s lack of top-level representation. 
Last year, when the Solomon Islands hosted the 54th PIF Leaders’ Meeting, all external partners were excluded. The stated reason was a review of partnership arrangements, but the practical effect was to remove Taiwan from a gathering it had attended as a development partner since 1992. This year, with Palau – which has official diplomatic ties with Taiwan – as host, the dynamics reversed. 
Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung arrived in Koror leading a delegation that included representatives from energy, technology, construction, and agriculture, and he met with Whipps, Palau’s president, to strengthen bilateral ties before participating in the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue. 
Only three PIF members still maintain formal ties with Taipei, but Taiwan’s development programs extend well beyond those allies. Just in July 2026, Taiwan donated $2 million to the Forum Secretariat and in 2025 it pledged $3 million to the Pacific Resilience Facility. 
Beijing, however, doesn’t take kindly to Taiwan’s inclusion in any form. China’s special envoy Qian Bo confronted Whipps directly at the Forum Troika meeting in Fiji, demanding Taiwan’s exclusion and warning that Beijing would “have to retaliate.” He dismissed Palau as “a small country.” Whipps was unfazed: “It doesn’t matter. We’re a country.” He later characterized Qian’s conduct as inappropriate, remarking that “if you want somebody to love you, usually you come with chocolates and nice cards.”
China made good on Qian’s threat on August 19, when Beijing’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism issued a travel advisory for Palau, warning of alleged theft and dangerous marine conditions and portraying one of the Pacific’s safest destinations as a place to avoid. The U.S. Embassy rejected the advisory, stating that “the United States opposes any attempts by China to weaponize tourism to coerce Palau.”
Tourism accounts for roughly 40 percent of Palau’s gross domestic product, and Beijing has used this lever before. After Palau refused to break ties with Taiwan, China banned package tours in 2017 and visitor numbers collapsed, but the country absorbed the shock and the weapon’s effectiveness has diminished with repeated use.
Whipps has been characteristically blunt about the situation “China continues to try to influence us, whether its threatening us with weaponizing tourism or attacking us personally,” he told reporters. “We’ve made it very clear from the beginning [that] nobody is going to tell us who our friends can be.”
Palau, with a population of roughly 18,000, has held its ground on Taiwan. Other Pacific Island states haven’t. Solomon Islands switched recognition to Beijing in 2019; Kiribati followed within weeks. Naoero switched in January 2024. Taiwan’s Pacific footprint has halved, going from six diplomatic partners in 2019 to just three today: the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu.
The PIF Leaders’ Meeting, of course, is about much more than Taiwan, or even China. The summit’s agenda includes a climate declaration ahead of COP31 and a new maritime anti-smuggling initiative called Waqa Moana. The Pacific Resilience Facility, with $173 million in pledges toward a $500 million target, represents a genuine institutional innovation as a Pacific-owned climate finance mechanism. 
But the credibility of a regional body rests on its capacity to address threats as well as opportunities. A forum that can mobilize around climate finance but cannot issue a statement when a nuclear-armed power tests a ballistic missile in its own members’ waters with barely any warning faces a fundamental question about what regional solidarity actually means. 
The empty chairs in Palau are symptoms of a regional order under pressure, one in which the line between domestic sovereignty and external manipulation grows harder to draw with each passing year.
The 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders’ Meeting opened on August 31 under a banner of unity, but it can’t escape the reality that outside powers are competing for influence in the Pacific. The question now facing the PIF is whether the forum’s consensus model, once a safeguard for small-state sovereignty, has become the very mechanism through which that influence reshapes regional outcomes.
The official theme of this year’s PIF Leaders’ Meeting, held in Palau, is B.E.L.A.U., or Building Economies, Life, Action, Unity, an acronym that doubles as a tribute to the host nation’s indigenous name. It was meant to signal collective resolve. Instead, the gathering has been defined by conspicuous absences and blocked consensus. Given the return of Taiwan as a development partner after last year’s exclusion, some see this year’s PIF as proof of Beijing’s growing capacity to paralyze the region’s most important multilateral institution from within.
At least five Pacific leaders chose not to attend. The leaders of Kiribati, Samoa, and Vanuatu dispatched deputies, while Fiji’s Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka stayed home to manage domestic affairs. The most dramatic absence was that of Solomon Islands’ Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who landed in Palau only to leave hours later after a no-confidence motion was filed against him back in Honiara. Wale had served as prime minister for barely three months and as outgoing PIF chair, was meant to hand the gavel to Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr. Instead, he left Foreign Minister Rick Hou to represent his country at the summit.
Kiribati’s case is particularly revealing. President Taneti Maamau dispatched not a cabinet minister but David Teaabo, his director of foreign service and a former ambassador to China. In an organization where decisions require consensus at the level of heads of state, sending a lower-ranking delegate who cannot commit to communique language with full authority is itself a political statement.

Beijing provided only a few hours’ notice to the affected Pacific Island nations.
The reaction was swift – at least from those countries that did respond. articles.title: A Deadly Flood Underscores the CCP-Imposed Information Vacuum in Tibet
articles.full_text:
The disaster exposed a stark contrast: open reporting is emerging from Nepal, while information from Tibet remains almost entirely dependent on China’s tightly controlled state media.
A screenshot of CCTV footage shows the moment that a massive mudslide engulfed the town of Gyirong in Tibet, China, Aug. 26, 2026.
The floods and landslides devastating communities in Tibet and Nepal are a natural disaster. The information vacuum inside Tibet is not.
Hundreds of people remain missing. Families are desperately searching for loved ones. Americans are among the foreign nationals reported unaccounted for. Roads, communications, and power have been cut, while rescue teams race to reach communities across some of the most difficult terrain in the world.
But on the Tibetan side of this disaster, there is another obstacle: the Chinese Communist Party’s longstanding restrictions on access and information.
For years, Beijing has tightly controlled access to Tibet for foreign journalists, diplomats, researchers, and independent organizations. In ordinary times, these restrictions keep the world from seeing Tibet. In a disaster, they can keep the world from understanding what Tibetans need, and potentially from helping them.
That is why Beijing should open affected Tibetan areas to the outside world.
Humanitarian organizations need to be able to safely reach communities and independently assess needs. Journalists need to be able to establish what is happening beyond official accounts. Foreign governments need timely information about their citizens and, where necessary, consular access. Families need to know what has happened to missing loved ones. And Tibetans themselves need to be able to tell the world what has happened to their communities and what they need.
Access is not an abstract human rights principle in an emergency. It is a lifeline.
President Xi Jinping has ordered an “all-out” search for the missing, and China has mobilized hundreds of rescuers in Tibet. But mobilizing the power of the state is not the same as permitting independent scrutiny. If Beijing is confident in its response, it should let the world see for itself.
The Himalayas may be divided by national borders, but their rivers, glaciers, and climate risks are not. This cross-border disaster has made that reality painfully clear. Not only did the flood devastate communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border, but authorities in Bihar, India moved people from vulnerable areas amid concern that floodwaters could eventually threaten communities farther downstream.
Timely sharing of hydrological, meteorological, glacial, and disaster-risk information is a matter of public safety. China should urgently engage with Nepal, India, and other governments across the Himalayan region to build durable, reliable, and accessible real-time information sharing and cross-border early-warning systems. No community should be left without potentially lifesaving information because a threat originates on the other side of an international border.
The disaster should also change how Washington thinks about access to Tibet. The U.S. Congress has long recognized that restrictions on Tibet have consequences for Americans. The Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act specifically cited the difficulties U.S. consular officials faced assisting Americans trapped in Tibet after the 2015 Nepal earthquake. Today, Americans are again among those reported missing in a disaster affecting the Nepal-Tibet border region.
The administration should press Beijing for timely information about missing Americans and seek whatever consular access may be necessary. It should ask whether independent humanitarian organizations can assess needs inside Tibet and whether affected communities are receiving adequate assistance.
Washington should also examine whether resources Congress has already made available for Tibetan communities can be rapidly mobilized to support the response.
And as the immediate rescue effort gives way to recovery, another question will become increasingly important: Will Tibetans have a meaningful voice in what happens next? Reconstruction should not become an excuse for forced relocation or development decisions imposed without meaningful consultation. Affected Tibetans should participate in decisions about rebuilding their communities, restoring livelihoods, and managing future disaster risks.
The forces of nature that brought devastation to the Himalayas were beyond Beijing’s control. The information vacuum and lack of access in Tibet is not.

articles.title: Micronesian Islands Meet Against Backdrop of Great Power Competition
articles.full_text:
Micronesian governments are elevating unilateral hedging efforts in forums like the MIF, in pursuit of a unified risk-management strategy and regional identity.
Leaders and Heads of Delegation at the 28th Micronesian Islands Forum.
From August 17 to 21, leaders and heads of delegation throughout the Micronesian subregion convened for the 28th Micronesian Islands Forum (MIF). Held in Pohnpei – one of four states of the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) and home to a population of roughly 26,000 people – delegates met to discuss ongoing regional issues and identified areas for strategic collaboration under the theme “Promote Healthy Communities, Open Doors to Learning.” 
I attended the MIF as the head of Delegation and Special Representative for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), a non-sovereign United States territory. As great powers pursue their foreign policy agendas, the event in Pohnpei revealed a continuing trend often overlooked in the Pacific: Micronesian governments are elevating unilateral hedging efforts in forums like the MIF, in pursuit of a unified risk-management strategy and regional identity. 
This year, the MIF met weeks before the more prominent Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders Meeting, which is being held in the neighboring Micronesian country of Palau from August 30 to September 4. Seated in the front row of the forum’s audience were senior members of the diplomatic corps posted in the FSM, including ambassadors representing Australia, China, and Japan, and the United States’ newest Chargé d’Affaires to Palikir, who arrived in the country just a week before the MIF. 
The venue itself was striking: the State of Pohnpei Administrative Building and Governor’s Office, built by Beijing in 2007 and renovated last year by the Chinese government and state-owned contractors. The Federated States of Micronesia have had formal diplomatic relations with Beijing since 1989, and is the only U.S. Freely Associated State – all of which are located in Micronesia – that maintains such a relationship.
China and the United States are not the only development partners competing in Pohnpei. Just two kilometers north of the Governor’s Office off the Dekehtik Causeway, Japan’s government is investing 4.6 billion yen ($30 million) in a project to expand the Pohnpei Port, the FSM’s primary maritime gateway. In the Pohnpeian outer island of Pingelap, Australia has financed a solar mini-grid and battery storage system for a geographically disconnected island community. These recent investments showcase the strategic importance of MIF member states to great powers and are not unique to FSM.
Similar practices can be found elsewhere across Micronesia. Foreign direct investment, infrastructure improvements, and diplomatic engagement have become increasingly visible in a region where small island economies are often balancing relationships with several development partners at once. For Micronesia, these relationships are not necessarily mutually exclusive. The same governments that have maintained a historically close partnership with the United States can pursue infrastructure and development partnerships with Japan, Australia, China, and others, depending on domestic needs and priorities.
The discussions held at the MIF centered around the outcomes of the forum’s several standing committees, including the approval of resolutions focused on U.S. deep sea mining efforts in Micronesia, the development of competitive commercial fisheries in Guam and the CNMI, and the financial stability of the forum itself. The latter action was arguably the most important to the MIF, functioning as a soft call to attending development partners and multilateral institutions for financial support. Member states underscored the need for sustainable funding to support a permanent secretariat, lifting the planning and implementation burden off of any future host government. The emphasis on establishing a more permanent institutional structure comes as Micronesian states continue to navigate their role within the broader Pacific regional infrastructure.
Five years ago, five Micronesian countries initiated the formal process to withdraw from the PIF after their supported candidate for the forum’s secretary-general position – a diplomat from the Marshall Islands – lost the body’s vote. The region instead decided to look inward, pursuing the strengthening of subregional collaboration. After reformation efforts in 2022 and 2023, those Micronesian nations rejoined the PIF, with the forum being held in the subregion for the first time since the 49th PIF in Nauru (now spelled Naoero) in 2018.
The history of that split remains relevant to the MIF today. The forum’s renewed focus on institutional sustainability is not only an administrative concern, but part of a broader effort to ensure that Micronesian governments have a regional mechanism through which they can coordinate their interests. Concurrently, the subregion’s reintegration into the PIF underscores that a robust MIF serves to complement, rather than contradict, expansive Pacific multilateralism.
This year’s PIF meeting further highlights the diplomatic complexity of Micronesia. Palau is hosting the meeting, with the Marshall Islands among the Micronesian states participating in the forum. Both countries maintain official diplomatic ties and a close relationship with Taiwan. Their participation comes as Micronesian governments continue to maintain contrasting relationships with the great powers active across the subregion, even as they pursue greater coordination on issues of common interest.
The timing of this year’s MIF, held two weeks before the PIF Leaders Meeting, provided an opportunity for Micronesian governments to coordinate ahead of the larger regional gathering. The standing committee outcomes raised in Pohnpei can be carried into discussions and actionable lines of effort in Palau. The proximity of the two meetings is particularly relevant this year, as the PIF returns to Micronesia. 
For the MIF, member states must work diligently to make the regional forum in its 28th iteration more durable. The return of Micronesian states to the Pacific Islands Forum has restored their participation in the broader Pacific community, while the continued development of the Micronesian Islands Forum provides a concentrated platform for Micronesia’s concerns. How effectively the forum can maintain that balance will largely depend on whether its members and development partners can provide the resources required to sustain it.
The attention surrounding this year’s meetings suggests that the stakes are becoming higher. Micronesia is receiving more development assistance and greater strategic interest from external powers. As ministers, diplomats, and development partners switch gears from Pohnpei to Palau, and as U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau leads Washington’s delegation to the 55th PIF, one thing remains clear: all eyes are on Micronesia.

articles.title: Kazakhstan’s New Parliament Appoints Tokayev’s Pick, Aibek Dadebay, as Chair
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan’s new unicameral parliament voted in favor of appointing the leader of the Adilet party, a close confidant of President Tokayev, as its first chairman.
One of the first points of action when Kazakhstan’s new unicameral parliament met for the first time on August 28 was the election of its speaker from among the 145 elected parliamentarians. The choice almost unanimously fell on the leader of the Adilet party, Aibek Dadebay, who had already been nominated for the position in advance by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. 
Adilet won more than 70 percent of the vote during the election, making it by far the largest party in the Kurultai with 110 seats. 
The new speaker has worked as an academic and diplomat over the past 25 years, most recently working within the country’s presidential administration. His career has been shaped by Tokayev, with whom he has worked since 2013, when the now-president chaired the Kazakh Senate. 
Despite technically being a new party in Kazakhstan, Adilet was quickly connected to other pro-presidential parties. Two months after its founding congress in May, Adilet experienced an immense boost in power as the Amanat party, which had dominated Kazakh politics for over 20 years (prior to 2022 under the name Nur-Otan), decided to merge with them. Besides boosting Adilet, the merger was also seen as a way to maintain the organizational structures of the senior party, while distancing it from its historic connections to former President Nursultan Nazarbayev. This was seen as necessary following the chaos that erupted in relation to the January 2022 events – also known as Qandy Qantar, or Bloody January.
Despite already being a close associate of Tokayev, it was in the aftermath of Qandy Qantar that Dadebay began work in the central presidential administration. Within a few years, he advanced to become head of the presidential administration. He was relieved of that post on May 5; just two days later, he was elected as chairman of Adilet. This decision, along with the ease with which the party was registered to run, led The Diplomat’s Catherine Putz to previously describe Adilet as “parroting the existing president’s platform.”
Just as Adilet inherited many of Amanat’s structures, it also posted a similar landslide parliamentary election result, gaining 71.17 percent of the votes on August 23. The OSCE, which observed the election, stated that this victory was secured due to an unfair advantage for Adilet that had blurred the line between the party and the Kazakh state.
Tokayev said that Adilet “bears great responsibility” when he spoke at the Kurultai’s opening session, before outlining what he saw as the parliament’s main tasks during this first mandate. Key in this description was for the parliament to “consolidate society around common interests and become a driving force for reform,” and, most importantly, “serve the interests of the state,” as the president said.
The outlined goal simultaneously aligned with the president’s nominee for the role of speaker, with Tokayev calling the 46-year-old Dadebay an “educated, patriotic, and responsible citizen” when advocating for his appointment. With the subsequent vote on Dadebay’s role as chairman turning out almost unanimously, Tokayev now stands with both a widely pro-presidential parliament and a long-term confidant overseeing its work going forward. With that, the president has also secured a swift procedure regarding the appointment of governmental figures, such as new prime ministers and vice presidents. On August 31, Tokayev named Erlan Karin, a longtime close advisor, to the new vice presidential post and reappointed Olzhas Bektenov to the prime ministership, which he’s held since February 2024.
While Kazakh law prohibits Tokayev from being a member of a political party, the recent election and subsequent appointment of central positions in the new unicameral parliament have shown that the president’s confidants still hold central power.

Just as Adilet inherited many of Amanat’s structures, it also posted a similar landslide parliamentary election result, gaining 71.17 percent of the votes on August 23. The OSCE, which observed the election, stated that this victory was secured due to an unfair advantage for Adilet that had blurred the line between the party and the Kazakh state.
Tokayev said that Adilet “bears great responsibility” when he spoke at the Kurultai’s opening session, before outlining what he saw as the parliament’s main tasks during this first mandate. Key in this description was for the parliament to “consolidate society around common interests and become a driving force for reform,” and, most importantly, “serve the interests of the state,” as the president said.
The outlined goal simultaneously aligned with the president’s nominee for the role of speaker, with Tokayev calling the 46-year-old Dadebay an “educated, patriotic, and responsible citizen” when advocating for his appointment. With the subsequent vote on Dadebay’s role as chairman turning out almost unanimously, Tokayev now stands with both a widely pro-presidential parliament and a long-term confidant overseeing its work going forward. With that, the president has also secured a swift procedure regarding the appointment of governmental figures, such as new prime ministers and vice presidents. On August 31, Tokayev named Erlan Karin, a longtime close advisor, to the new vice presidential post and reappointed Olzhas Bektenov to the prime ministership, which he’s held since February 2024.
While Kazakh law prohibits Tokayev from being a member of a political party, the recent election and subsequent appointment of central positions in the new unicameral parliament have shown that the president’s confidants still hold central power.
One of the first points of action when Kazakhstan’s new unicameral parliament met for the first time on August 28 was the election of its speaker from among the 145 elected parliamentarians. The choice almost unanimously fell on the leader of the Adilet party, Aibek Dadebay, who had already been nominated for the position in advance by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. 
Adilet won more than 70 percent of the vote during the election, making it by far the largest party in the Kurultai with 110 seats. 
Albert Otkjær is a journalist focusing on post-Soviet countries.
articles.summary: Kazakhstan’s new unicameral parliament voted in favor of appointing the leader of the Adilet party, a close confidant of President Tokayev, as its first chairman.

articles.title: Hitting a High Point: The Australia-Indonesia 2+2
articles.full_text:
The significance of the 2+2 is the growing web of cooperation between Canberra and Jakarta.
Last week, Australia and Indonesia held their tenth 2+2 defense and foreign ministers meeting in Melbourne. The two countries signed the landmark Jakarta Treaty on Common Security in 2024, and although the Indonesian parliament has yet to ratify the treaty, the 2+2 meeting proceeded with the assumption that this is simply the pace of Indonesia’s legislative processes, and that discussions can turn to how best to operationalize their cooperation. 
The headline claim is that the relationship between the two countries is now “at a high point.” The Albanese government has made the relationship with Indonesia one of the central pillars of Australia’s foreign policy, understanding how vital friendly, cooperative, relations with its giant near neighbor is to the country’s security. Indonesia, for its part, has recognized it has a capable partner in Canberra that can help advance its own security interests, while maintaining its strategic autonomy. 
Although the two countries are seeking to broaden their relationship, at present, defense and security cooperation remain the core elements and these areas were naturally a major focus of the discussions last week. 
Given the nature of their geographies, this has developed into a focus on maritime security. At the 2+2 meeting it was announced that Australia will provide aerial drones and training to Indonesia’s Coast Guard. Given that illegal fishing is a central concern throughout Indonesia’s vast waters, and that Chinese often use maritime militia disguised as fishing vessels, greater maritime domain awareness is considered essential for Jakarta. 
Alongside this, Australia and Indonesia agreed to increase cooperation on cybercrime, critical infrastructure, and artificial intelligence, building on their existing memorandum of understanding on enhanced cybersecurity and critical technology cooperation. This includes incorporating a defensive cybersecurity component into their bilateral defense exercise, Keris Woomera. Here, cybersecurity is not treated as a separate technical issue, but as a central pillar of military preparedness and national defense.
There is a similar thinking around economic security as inseparable from traditional security. The ministers announced a number of initiatives designed to make their economies more resilient to external shocks and any disruption to supply chains. This included new cooperation to jointly analyze critical supply chain issues and new scholarship courses that will be focused on economic security and resilience – hoping to develop a new cohort of analysts and bureaucrats focused on these issues. 
The two countries have already demonstrated how economic interdependence can provide security benefits, with Indonesia working with Australian industry to facilitate a 250,000-tonne agricultural-grade supply of urea due to disruptions from the war in Iran. Alongside this, Australian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) exports to Indonesia have increased threefold over the past year, again in response to supply chain disruptions in the Middle East. 
These practical forms of food and energy security are becoming increasingly intertwined with geopolitics. The two countries therefore have an interest in using the resources of one another to address their vulnerabilities. Given both their proximity to each other, and their current distance from global hotspots, there is an opportunity to build resilience together that can withstand any global shocks. 
These shocks include the environment. The 2+2 meeting announced the second phase of KINETIK – the Australia-Indonesia Climate and Sustainable Infrastructure Partnership, which will provide US$430 million over ten years to support sustainable infrastructure and climate investment in Indonesia. Its aim is to mobilize public and private capital into clean energy, water, waste management, and sustainable transport, helping Indonesia build climate-resilient infrastructure and accelerate its energy transition. With the hope of the two countries also developing their green technology capabilities. 
The 2+2 meeting also demonstrated considered strategic alignment over the regional order – something that hasn’t always been the case. The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to international law, sovereignty and ASEAN centrality, with both expressing concern about rising tensions in the South China Sea and insisting that the Code of Conduct being developed by ASEAN and China must comply with international law. 
The significance of the 2+2 is the growing web of cooperation between Canberra and Jakarta. From defense exercises to maritime surveillance to cybersecurity and economic resilience, there has been a noticeable step up in the relationship. This does not amount to a formal alliance, but more a convergence of interests and a recognition that as neighbors there is a natural interconnectedness. The previous distance in outlook and coordination is starting to be overcome.

articles.title: What Zheng He’s Changing Role Reveals About China’s Maritime Strategy
articles.full_text:
The historical figure has been invoked to advance different symbolic ends as Beijing’s goals and capabilities change.
A statue of Zheng He in Changle, Fuzhou Province, China.
The Ming Dynasty navigator Zheng He is often closely associated with Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road narrative. But the historical figure has been used as a diplomatic tool for decades, long before Xi launched the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
Zheng He entered the diplomatic storytelling of the People’s Republic of China within a decade of its founding. Under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao he became part of a broader historical argument about China’s rise, a role that remained prominent during the first years of Xi’s presidency. 
Much attention has been paid to why Beijing revived Zheng He. But few have noticed how mentions of Zheng He changed: Since 2018, China’s top leaders have increasingly moved away from using him to argue that a stronger China would not become a conquering power. 
As early as the late Qing period, Chinese nationalists recast Zheng He as evidence that China had once possessed global reach. During the Republican era he entered Chinese history textbooks and became a domestic symbol of national capacity. Around the time of the Bandung Conference, Beijing began recoding him for diplomacy. Zheng He was increasingly presented as a powerful but anti-colonial emissary of Afro-Asian friendship, particularly in China’s relations with newly independent African states.
Under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao, China’s top leaders systematically invoked Zheng He in diplomatic settings to answer a question at the heart of China’s rise: How would a China that was becoming powerful again use its power? In 2003, while explaining China’s “peaceful rise and development” at Harvard University, Wen described Zheng He as a diplomat who had sought friendly relations with other countries across seven voyages, tying this history directly to the Chinese tradition of loving peace. 
In 2005, speaking to the Mexican Senate, Hu again used the Silk Road and Zheng He’s voyages as historical evidence of China’s commitment to peaceful development. In Pretoria in 2007, Hu invoked Zheng He before turning to China’s own experience of colonialism to argue that China would not impose its will on Africa. 
The logic of Hu’s argument rested on an asymmetry of power. A fleet incapable of conquest proves nothing by refraining from violence. Only if the fleet is understood to possess the capacity to conquer can its peaceful approach serve as evidence of restraint. To Chinese leaders, Zheng He’s story showed how China would exercise superior power without undertaking conquest. Beijing drew on this argument particularly when it sought to reassure foreign audiences about how China would use its growing power, including in its diplomacy with African, Southeast Asian, and Arab states.
This usage persisted for a while after Xi took office. In 2014, Xi placed Zheng He directly within his argument that the Chinese nation carries “no gene for invading others or seeking hegemony.” At the first Belt and Road Forum in 2017, Xi listed Zheng He alongside Zhang Qian, Du Huan, Marco Polo, and Ibn Battuta as friendly envoys along the Silk Road. As the Maritime Silk Road became central to Xi-era diplomacy, Zheng He remained an obvious historical resource.
The later Premier Li Keqiang was especially consistent in bringing up Zheng He during this period. At the 2015 China-ASEAN Leaders’ Meeting and the East Asia Summit, Li invoked the navigator to argue that the South China Sea had been a sea of peace and freedom of navigation for six centuries. Three years later, at the 2018 East Asia Summit, Li was still using Zheng He in much the same way.
After 2018, however, the pattern of top-level use began to change. The decline was most visible in the field of regional maritime order, where references to Zheng He had once figured prominently. At the 2019 East Asia Summit, Li addressed similar regional issues without invoking Zheng He. By the 2023 Belt and Road Forum, even the language of civilizational exchange and connectivity no longer required name-dropping Zheng He. 
One contributing factor may have been the 2016 South China Sea arbitration, which made historical arguments about maritime rights more legally awkward. But the timing does not line up perfectly. Two years after the ruling, Li was still making much the same argument. Instead, the break came in 2019, which means the arbitration alone cannot account for it.
China’s maritime strategy and naval capabilities were themselves changing. In 2012, the 18th Party Congress formally called for China to become a “maritime power.” Three years later, the defense white paper China’s Military Strategy directed the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) to move from a posture centered on “offshore waters defense” toward a combination of “offshore waters defense” and “open seas protection.” 
At celebrations marking the PLAN’s 70th anniversary in Qingdao in 2019, Xi introduced the idea of a “maritime community with a shared future.” He also stressed that China followed a defensive national defense policy and that the navy would safeguard international sea lanes, shoulder international responsibilities, and provide more public goods for maritime security. 
The U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 China Military Power Report describes the PLAN as fielding Asia’s largest force of principal surface combatants, submarines, and amphibious warfare ships. As China built aircraft carriers, sustained far-seas escort missions, established overseas support facilities, and expanded its shipbuilding capacity, Beijing increasingly shifted the basis of its reassurance from historical precedent toward declared policy and contemporary behavior.
The growth of China’s naval capabilities reduced Zheng He’s value as evidence of maritime power. It also changed the analogy itself. In the 2000s, the official narrative constructed by Hu and Wen used Zheng He to show that maritime capability and peaceful intent could coexist. But by the late 2010s, China’s expanding naval power had become an observable reality, increasingly open to judgment through the navy’s actual conduct. The more the Zheng He narrative linked formidable maritime power with voluntary restraint, the more it invited foreign audiences to apply the same standard to China today. The analogy had therefore become more politically demanding.
Zheng He still appears, but mostly in bilateral settings to discuss historical ties with specific countries or communities. In April 2025, Xi’s signed article in the Malaysian press mentioned sites in Malacca associated with Zheng He. On April 21, 2026, during a meeting with Mozambican President Daniel Chapo, Xi noted that Zheng He’s fleet had visited the Mozambican coast more than six centuries earlier. In June of the same year, the Chinese embassy in Tanzania again presented Zheng He’s voyages as a historical symbol of long-standing exchanges between Chinese and Swahili civilizations. Later that month, Jakarta launched a series of cultural exchanges under the banner of “Zheng He’s Voyage: Envoys of Friendship.” In these settings, Zheng He primarily serves as a marker of shared history. In that sense, Beijing is returning Zheng He to the more limited diplomatic role he played in the 1950s and 1960s.
Zheng He’s visibility remains high. Exhibitions in Jakarta and Nairobi marked the 620th anniversary of his voyages; an academy in Angola now bears his name, as do international freight links. But in recent top-level diplomacy, he no longer serves primarily as evidence of China’s national character. 
That retreat has also made the difference between Zheng He and another historical icon, Zhang Qian, easier to see. Zhang Qian, the Han Dynasty envoy sent to the Western Regions, has long been regarded as a pioneer of the overland Silk Road. Compared with Zheng He, he represents the active opening of new routes and spaces for exchange. Existing discussions often treat the two as equivalent historical precursors of the Belt and Road. Yet Zhang Qian cannot easily perform Zheng He’s old role of providing reassurance as to China’s peaceful intentions.
The shift has also been uneven across Zheng He’s main diplomatic settings. He appears to have receded more sharply in Africa than in Southeast Asia. In its diplomacy with Africa, Beijing increasingly draws on 20th century anti-colonial solidarity and the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation to narrate historical ties. In Southeast Asia, by contrast, physical sites associated with Zheng He in Malacca, local memories of his voyages, and the Maritime Silk Road continue to sustain a highly localized political afterlife for the navigator.
Another round of China-ASEAN leaders’ meetings and the East Asia Summit will take place this November, while Shenzhen will host the APEC summit in the same month. Whether Zheng He reappears will be worth watching. If Beijing invokes him again, the more revealing question will be what it asks him to prove this time: restraint six centuries ago, or simply a shared local past.

articles.title: Sri Lanka’s Luxury Property Boom Is Outrunning Its Regulations
articles.full_text:
As Colombo’s luxury towers rise, the laws and institutions meant to oversee them lag far behind. Financial history shows that rarely ends well.
A few months back, two of Sri Lanka’s largest real estate companies launched two apartment projects in Colombo Port City, reclaimed land in Colombo developed by China Harbor Engineering Company (CHEC) as a joint venture with Sri Lankan government. One was a residential development project while the other is a luxury twin residential tower in Central Park district in port city.
The pitch to buyers was simple and very tempting: invest in an apartment and get a higher return. One company advertising slogan promised that if you invest today, you will double your money in four years, “guaranteed.” It is an appealing proposition, promising a very high return, expected to be made through property price speculation. 
These are not the only real estate projects in Colombo Port City. Before these two real estate agencies launched their projects, another leading construction company launched another luxury apartment project in Port City. Together, these three real estate projects have estimated value of $650 million. 
The investments for all three projects came from local companies. After years of struggle, Colombo Port City is now receiving considerable investments. By April this year, Sri Lanka’s Cabinet of Ministers had approved 77 Businesses of Strategic Importance (BSIs) to operate in Colombo Port City and had attracted investments worth $2.19 billion to date. 
Luxury apartments are, however, not just confined to Colombo Port City. They are booming in many areas of Colombo, Sri Lanka’s commercial capital and largest city. Most of these luxury apartment projects are advertised as investment opportunities. The Central Bank’s condominium market survey for the first quarter of 2026 shows that more than 20 percent of condominiums are purchased for investment, and that high-end units account for a growing share of sales. Nearly 52 percent of condominiums sold were valued at more than 50 million rupees ($150,000). Such high-end apartments accounted for only 33 percent of apartment sales a year ago. 
An apartment in Colombo Port City costs about $500,000 and up. These prices are expected to increase substantively in coming years, allowing those who purchase apartments to sell at a higher price and make a substantial return. Sri Lanka’s apartment projects have now transformed into a speculative investment dominated by buyers chasing price appreciation rather than genuine housing need. While this is also the case in places like Dubai, Sri Lanka’s regulations on real estate industry or the government institutions are not built for such a speculative driven industry. 
When property is treated as an investment, the promised return depends on price appreciation. Rental yields on new luxury apartments have been rising, but they come nowhere near the allure of doubling the underlying asset value. The money, in other words, is made through speculation on asset prices rather than steady rental income. That is normal for real estate everywhere, but a speculation-driven market carries risks that are usually contained through strong oversight, well-designed regulation, and strict enforcement by capable state institutions. Sri Lanka has almost none of these.
In plain terms, Sri Lanka’s luxury real estate industry is expanding far faster than the government’s capacity to regulate or monitor it. That is a serious macroeconomic risk, and financial history shows that an unregulated property boom rarely ends well.
The body nominally responsible for apartment blocks in Sri Lanka is the Condominium Management Authority (CMA), which oversees the country’s luxury apartments, including those in Port City. But the CMA was never built to regulate speculation-driven investment property, and it does not have the capacity to do so.
The authority began life as the Common Amenities Board, created under a 1973 law to perform the narrow task of looking after the shared parts of apartment buildings, such as lifts, water, drainage, and common areas. A 2003 amendment renamed it and broadened its remit, but its core job remained that of a caretaker for completed buildings. It was never meant to be financial regulator for a fast-moving, pre-sales market worth hundreds of millions of dollars. 
As a result, many standard practices that are required to oversee a speculative-based real estate market are not incorporated into Sri Lankan law, and not practiced by the CMA. 
One such standard practice in large-scale real estate markets, like in Dubai, is to tie every project to an escrow account under the regulator’s supervision. Dubai’s Law No. 8 of 2007 made such accounts compulsory for any apartment sale. Under this law, buyers’ payments go into a ring-fenced account (referred to as the escrow account), and the Dubai Land Department (DLD) approves releasing the next tranche of money in the escrow account only after it verifies that construction has genuinely progressed. A developer cannot dip into those funds to meet other cash-flow needs. This protects investors and limits the financial risk to the wider economy.
Sri Lankan law requires nothing of the sort. Escrow accounts are left entirely to developers’ discretion. Thus, the money paid by buyers is not guaranteed to be spent on the project or its progress. Most developers, including some of those constructing apartments in Colombo Port City, choose to do projects without escrow accounts. Therefore, when a buyer makes an up-front or monthly payment, that money does not go into a protected account; it flows straight into the developer’s general finances, to be spent as the company sees fit.
For the individual buyer, the danger is obvious: if a project stalls or a developer collapses, the money can simply vanish. For the economy, the picture is worse. Developers are effectively borrowing from ordinary buyers without the scrutiny a bank lending the same sums would face, and the failure of one project could ripple across a developer’s other projects and trigger a domino effect through the industry. This is exactly what happened in China, where developers like Evergrande used home buyers’ money to pay down debts from other projects – leaving buyers stuck with mortgages on forever-unfinished apartments. The resulting crisis dragged down the entire real estate sector, and China’s economy.
Embedding escrow accounts into law is therefore not merely desirable but considered as an essential regulatory practice to ensure the stability of the growing real estate industry, and overall economy. Sri Lanka has not made that regulatory change. 
India, in contrast, made this regulatory leap in 2016 through the introduction of Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA), which made escrow accounts compulsory and established property data portals in each state to ensure transparency. Sri Lanka has no legislative requirement that mandates transparency on property sales, progress, or even licensing brokers and advertising. 
Lack of transparency had allowed Sri Lanka’s developers to broadcast eye-catching sales figures to stimulate demand and justify price increases while buyers have no means to check those claims. One real estate developer company, for instance, claimed that 50 percent of its Port City twin-tower project had sold ahead of launch. But there is no way to verify this, or any of the claims made by real estate developers, brokers, or sellers. There is no authoritative public record of what is being sold, at what price, or how far each project has been built. There are no regulations mandating developers to disclose the data, or make project progress publicly available. 
While luxury real estate industry is expanding fast, Sri Lanka is lagging behind the standard practice of transparency in real estate industry. For example, Dubai has a public register of real estate projects updated daily, through which any buyer can verify a transaction, and check units sold, valuations, and developer details. Sri Lanka policymakers as well as businesses claims that they aims to follow the footsteps of Dubai, and aspire to become a real estate hub in South Asia. However, Sri Lanka has not followed Dubai’s steps in setting up regulations, laws, or government institutions to facilitate a luxury real estate industry. 
Sri Lanka is, in effect, running a sophisticated, foreign-currency-denominated property market with the only oversight provided by a glorified residents’ association administrator. It simply has no capacity to regulate or oversee the rapidly expanding speculative real estate market in Colombo. 
The fixes are not mysterious. Sri Lanka needs a law to regulate the fast-growing luxury real estate industry, and set up institutions with sufficient capacity to implement regulations. India did this ten years ago with the introduction of RERA. Such a law needs to make escrow accounts compulsory for pre-completion sales and to bring advertising under regulatory guidelines. Sri Lanka also need to set up an online register of projects on the Dubai model, so sales, prices, and project status can be independently verified. It must create a new regulator, with the powers, staff, and expertise to license developers, scrutinize their marketing, and monitor their accounts, alongside a mechanism to tax capital gains on apartment price appreciation.
None of this can wait. The promise of “up to 100 percent gain” in four years is a textbook sign of speculation, and speculation can inflate a bubble whose collapse spills into the wider economy. Sri Lanka learned in 2022 how weak institutions and poor governance lead to economic disaster. Its luxury real estate is now expanding faster than the state’s ability to watch it, and the government must act before this boom becomes the next crisis.
