articles.title: Takaichi Is No Abe: Japan’s New Conservative Politics
articles.full_text:
After roughly 10 months in power, the differences between Takaichi and Abe are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
Japan’s Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae offers flowers and a prayer at the memorial for the late Abe Shinzo, former prime minister of Japan, in the Canberra Nara Peace Park, Canberra, Australia, May 4, 2026.
For many years, Japan’s current Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has been portrayed by international media as the heir to Abe Shinzo’s political legacy. Her nationalist views, assertive security posture, and close ties to Japan’s conservative movement have made the comparison seem natural. 
There is good reason for the comparison. As Michael Green recently argued in Foreign Affairs, Takaichi has continued an important part of Abe’s strategic legacy: strengthening Japan’s defense capabilities, deepening the Japan-U.S. alliance, and responding more assertively to the challenge posed by China. From this perspective, Takaichi represents the continuation of a strategy that seeks to make Japan a stronger and more indispensable U.S. ally.
But strategic continuity should not be confused with political continuity. After roughly 10 months in power, the differences between Takaichi and Abe are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Rather than simply reviving “Abe politics,” Takaichi appears to be developing a new political style of her own: more personalized, more confrontational, and more dependent on emotional mobilization through social media. If Abe represented a conservative politics tempered by strategic pragmatism, Takaichi may represent something closer to a new form of conservative populism. 
In other words, Takaichi may be Abe’s heir in grand strategy, but she is not necessarily adopting his tactics. The political methods emerging from Takaichi’s camp suggest a significant change in how Japan’s conservatives seek to mobilize domestic public support. 
The controversy over the use of artificial intelligence (AI) during the 2025 Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) leadership election and the 2026 House of Representatives election offers a revealing example. Shukan Bunshun, a Japanese weekly magazine known for exposing political scandals, recently reported that people close to Takaichi’s camp had used AI to produce large numbers of short videos attacking political opponents and circulated them widely online. The revelations triggered a public backlash and created the first serious political challenge of Takaichi’s premiership.
The use of digital technology for political campaigning is hardly unprecedented. What is more significant is how the technology appears to have been used: not simply to communicate policy positions or mobilize supporters, but to amplify political antagonism and shape voters’ emotions. During the Abe era, the prime minister’s office was highly sophisticated in managing the media and political narrative, but Abe generally maintained a clearer distinction between political messaging and outright mobilization through antagonism.
Takaichi’s political operation appears more willing to blur that boundary. This is particularly important because Takaichi has cultivated a direct relationship with voters through social media. Rather than relying primarily on Japan’s established media organizations, she uses X to communicate directly with the public. 
According to the Financial Times, Japanese business leaders have become increasingly frustrated with what they see as Takaichi’s unwillingness to listen to views from outside her political circle. They are also concerned that she has become increasingly hostile toward the mainstream media while relying more heavily on social media to maintain her popularity. This approach may be politically effective in the short term. But it also carries potential risks. Social media rewards confrontation, immediacy, and emotional intensity. A political leader who relies heavily on such platforms can easily find herself governing through the logic of mobilization rather than the logic of consensus-building.
A second concern is the uncertainty surrounding Takaichi’s decision-making. In April, the Japanese magazine Sentaku reported that Takaichi had clashed with Imai Nobuya, a senior political adviser during the Abe era, over the possible deployment of the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to the Middle East. According to the report, Imai opposed Takaichi’s reported intention to send Japanese forces to the Strait of Hormuz to support U.S. military operations against Iran. 
The details of the episode remain disputed, and the report should therefore be treated with caution. But the broader question it raises is difficult to dismiss: Does Takaichi have the same capacity for institutional and strategic balancing that characterized Abe’s leadership?
Abe was undoubtedly a committed conservative. Yet he was also an unusually pragmatic political operator. He relied heavily on trusted bureaucrats and political advisers, and he understood the importance of reconciling political ideology with institutional constraints and strategic realities. On major security and foreign policy questions, his administration typically sought to balance competing interests before making consequential decisions. 
Takaichi’s approach appears more personal. Her foreign policy positions are often closely associated with her own ideological convictions, and she has shown less evidence of the cautious political calibration that was one of Abe’s defining characteristics.
Nowhere is this difference more consequential than in relations with China. Abe is frequently described outside Japan as a China hawk. That description is not entirely wrong, but it misses an important and delicate part of his diplomacy. Despite his nationalist reputation, Abe repeatedly demonstrated an ability to separate ideological commitments from strategic interests. In April 2018, for example, according to a memoir written by a Taiwanese political figure, Abe declined to meet former Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui, who was staying at the same hotel in Okinawa, apparently to avoid unnecessarily provoking Beijing. 
In 2019, Abe also sent a private letter to Yasukuni Shrine exploring the possibility of removing the enshrined Class-A war criminals, an effort that would have reduced one of the most persistent sources of friction in Japan’s relations with its neighbors. (I learned of this episode in 2025 while interviewing Kitaoka Shinichi, one of Abe’s key foreign policy advisers, at Stanford University.) 
Whatever one thinks of Abe’s broader political legacy, these episodes demonstrate that his conservatism was accompanied by a strong instinct for strategic risk management. He understood that nationalist symbolism could generate domestic political benefits while imposing substantial diplomatic costs.
Takaichi has yet to demonstrate the same degree of restraint. Her approach to China appears to be driven more directly by ideological convictions and political instincts than by a broader strategy for managing Japan’s long-term relationship with its most important neighboring power. 
This is precisely where the distinction between Takaichi and Abe becomes most important. Abe sought to strengthen Japan’s alliance with the United States while simultaneously maintaining channels for stable relations with China. His foreign policy was not simply “tough” or “soft”; it was fundamentally about strategic management.
If Takaichi is indeed continuing Abe’s grand strategy by strengthening the Japan-U.S. alliance and making Japan more capable of confronting China, that does not necessarily mean that she is reproducing Abe’s broader approach to statecraft. Abe’s strategic vision depended not only on strengthening Japan’s position, but also on managing the risks created by that stronger position.
Even some of the architects of Abe’s foreign policy now appear concerned about the direction of Japanese diplomacy. On July 2, Yachi Shotaro, the former head of Japan’s National Security Secretariat, wrote in his Nikkei series “My Life History” that the most important challenge facing Japanese diplomacy in the 21st century is its relationship with China. Japan, he argued, must think over the medium and long term about how to build a stable and strategic relationship with China while remaining a U.S. ally and recognizing China as an important neighboring country.
Yachi is hardly a dove on China. After Abe returned to power in 2006, he played a central role in efforts to improve China-Japan relations. According to interview records cited in journalist Funabashi Yoichi’s 2024 book on politics during the Abe era, “Children of Destiny,” Yachi also accompanied former Prime Minister Fukuda Yasuo to China in 2014 and helped facilitate the resumption of China-Japan summit diplomacy. 
His remarks therefore reveal something important about the Abe-era foreign-policy establishment. Its members may have supported a stronger Japan and a more robust alliance with Washington, but they also understood that strategic competition with China could not substitute for diplomacy. For them, managing the relationship with Beijing was an essential component of Japanese diplomatic statecraft.
Takaichi’s politics appear to place greater emphasis on confrontation. That difference may ultimately determine whether her premiership can endure. A June poll by Jiji Press put Takaichi’s approval rating at roughly 54 percent, down from around 70 percent at the beginning of the year. For a prime minister who has not yet fully consolidated her political authority, this is hardly an unassailable position. A major scandal, economic setback, or diplomatic crisis could quickly weaken her support.
Takaichi may share Abe’s nationalism, his skepticism toward the postwar liberal order, and his determination to strengthen Japan’s security posture. She may also continue many of the strategic policies that Michael Green and other scholars have associated with Abe’s legacy. But political inheritance is about more than policy positions. It is also about governing instincts.
Abe understood that conservative politics could be sustained only by combining ideology with pragmatism, nationalism with diplomacy, and political mobilization with institutional management. Takaichi appears to be experimenting with a different formula – one that places greater emphasis on personal leadership, social media politics, emotional mobilization, and confrontation with perceived political and cultural opponents.
That does not necessarily mean Takaichi will fail. Indeed, such a political style may prove highly effective in an era of fragmented media and growing public distrust of established institutions. Nor does it mean that Takaichi’s foreign policy is fundamentally incompatible with Abe’s. On the contrary, she may succeed in making Japan an even stronger U.S. ally. But a stronger Japan and a more predictable Japan are not necessarily the same thing.
U.S. policymakers should recognize that Japan is entering a new political era. The question of whether Takaichi is Abe’s successor is ultimately a distraction. What matters is whether she can turn her personalized style of conservative politics into an effective governing system. If she can, Japan’s conservatives may have found a new political formula – one that combines strategic nationalism with populist mobilization and direct communication with voters. If she cannot, the same forces that made Takaichi powerful could also make her government increasingly unstable and expose Japan to unnecessary security risks.
For many years, Japan’s current Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has been portrayed by international media as the heir to Abe Shinzo’s political legacy. Her nationalist views, assertive security posture, and close ties to Japan’s conservative movement have made the comparison seem natural. 
There is good reason for the comparison. As Michael Green recently argued in Foreign Affairs, Takaichi has continued an important part of Abe’s strategic legacy: strengthening Japan’s defense capabilities, deepening the Japan-U.S. alliance, and responding more assertively to the challenge posed by China. From this perspective, Takaichi represents the continuation of a strategy that seeks to make Japan a stronger and more indispensable U.S. ally.

articles.title: Can Discussions in Cambridge Help Afghans Build a Post-Taliban Future?
articles.full_text:
Thousands of miles from Afghanistan, prescriptions are being written by Afghans for the country’s future – a future without Taliban rule.
In the past, too many plans for Afghanistan have been designed far from the people expected to live under them. On the surface, the Cambridge Afghanistan Series, organized by the Mosaic Global Foundation, may seem to be more of the same. But the series is genuinely attempting something different, which is not to hand people of Afghanistan another foreign-made political formula, but to create a space in which Afghans themselves can identify the principles, institutions, and sequence required to reclaim their political future.
On September 4 and 5, the Mosaic Global Foundation will convene the fifth Cambridge Afghanistan Series (CAS V) at Jesus College, Cambridge. It will bring together Afghan political voices, civil society actors, human rights advocates, academics, and other stakeholders to discuss pathways toward peace, inclusion, and prosperity. 
At CAS III in 2024, six major political factions, including two major armed resistance groups, presented their visions for Afghanistan. An independent examination found that, despite their public divisions, more than 90 percent of their proposals overlapped in substance. CAS IV in 2025 began a more open discussion of the remaining disagreements.
I participated in CAS IV in 2025. I did not see complete unity, nor did I expect it. Afghanistan’s political actors carry different histories, represent different constituencies, bear different grievances, and have different ideas about the state. What I saw was something more modest but genuinely hopeful as major political currents, civil society, and human rights advocates from different ethnic backgrounds and communities gathered to discuss the future of their country and search for an Afghan-led solution. 
At a time when the Taliban has tried to erase political plurality inside Afghanistan, the sight of Afghans arguing across their differences, without denying one another a place in the conversation, offered a glimpse of another political culture. At CAS IV Afghans discussed a wide range of topics tied to the future of their country while celebrating their culture with traditional food and music on a night they named “Poetry Night.”     
A working group, facilitated by Mosaic, produced a Comprehensive Composite Roadmap, or CCR, at CAS IV in 2025.
The CCR emerged from a process that began at CAS III in 2024. Six major political groups were invited to present their strategic proposals, while an expert panel reviewed 12 roadmaps and proposals in total. The dialogue revealed more than 90 percent overlap among these initiatives in their strategic positions. An independent assessment commissioned by Mosaic subsequently confirmed this finding.
Following that assessment, an Independent Working Group was formed to consolidate the different proposals. It gathered in total 21 roadmaps and proposals from political groups, civil society organizations, and resistance groups and synthesized them into the CCR.
Ahead of CAS V in 2026, the consultation process is continuing and expanding to include specialists, human rights organizations, and religious scholars, or ulema. The aim is to ensure that the CCR incorporates contributions from all strata of Afghan society and reflects as comprehensive and inclusive a range of perspectives as possible.
The CCR rests on three non-negotiable commitments: Afghanistan must have a government chosen by its people, human rights must be respected, and equality – including gender equality – must be guaranteed. Around those commitments, it proposes a broader transition based on national dialogue, regional peace dialogues, and international consensus through a United Nations-led process.
Its central mechanism is a proposed Political Convergence Framework. This would bring together anti-Taliban armed resistance groups, political parties and platforms, civil society and human rights organizations, women’s movements, religious scholars, youth, journalists, professional groups, and diaspora representatives. Its initial responsibilities would include adopting a founding charter, creating a joint secretariat, drafting a detailed transition plan, coordinating internal resistance and civil action, and conducting regional and international diplomacy.
The roadmap then envisages an international conference, the creation of a preparatory committee, the formation of a representative Constituent Assembly, and a merit-based transitional government. The Constituent Assembly would help draft a new constitution and provide legal oversight during the transition. The transitional government would maintain order, build institutions, prepare free elections, and transfer authority to a government elected by the people.
The reason behind this sequencing is the belief that removing the Taliban, by itself, would not answer the fundamental questions that have repeatedly destabilized Afghanistan: Who possesses political authority? How is that authority distributed? How are citizens protected from domination by the state or by one another? How can ethnic, linguistic, religious, and gender diversity be reflected without reducing politics to permanent communal quotas?
To my knowledge, no other current Afghanistan initiative has undertaken this particular task at comparable breadth: placing competing roadmaps side by side, identifying their shared core, preserving the questions that remain disputed, and trying to convert overlapping principles into a common mechanism for action. 
Afghanistan’s own recent history provides the clearest warning of why such an initiative is necessary. In 2001, for instance, the Bonn process reduced political reconstruction to a mechanical redistribution of power and a quota system for elite rotation. This meant distributing government positions and political influence among a limited circle of established figures and groups, based on negotiated shares, rather than constructing a genuinely representative system grounded in broad citizen participation, public consent, and accountable institutions. Whatever institutions a conference may establish, an elite bargain is not the same as a durable social contract. CAS must not reproduce another closed agreement among familiar figures in a different foreign conference room. It must connect political negotiation to citizen rights, representative institutions, public accountability, and a fair process for deciding the country’s constitutional future.
Nor should the claim of 90 percent agreement be allowed to conceal the difficult 10 percent where groups disagree. The collected roadmaps still differ over centralization and decentralization, engagement with the Taliban versus struggle against it, the proper role of international actors, the meaning of territorial integrity, and the mechanisms required to correct structural inequality. These are not minor questions. They concern the distribution of power and the identity of the future Afghan state.
That is why CAS V must commit to show how representatives are selected, how women and communities inside Afghanistan influence decisions, how disagreements are recorded, and how the process will communicate with Afghans who cannot enter the Jesus College halls. Women cannot be present merely as symbols while established male politicians negotiate over authority. Civil society cannot be used to decorate a settlement reached elsewhere without them. Those exposed to repression inside Afghanistan must have secure and meaningful channels into the process. Without such commitments, CAS V will become another annual discussion. With them, Cambridge could become the place where the fragmented Afghanistan opposition begins to acquire institutional form.
A conference in Cambridge cannot, on its own, end Taliban rule. A roadmap cannot substitute for political organization inside Afghanistan, nor can international recognition manufacture domestic legitimacy. But the absence of a coherent alternative has long weakened Afghan democratic forces and enabled outside actors to treat Taliban rule as the only available reality. The CCR challenges that fatalism.
The true measure of CAS V will be whether those gathered can establish a fair process for acting together while continuing to disagree. Afghanistan does not need another self-appointed ruler or another elite pact build thousands of miles away. It needs a legitimate path through which its people can recover the right to choose. If the Cambridge Afghanistan Series can help build that path, then a conversation taking place thousands of miles away may still belong, unmistakably, to Afghanistan.

articles.title: The Kuril Flashpoint: Putin’s Visit and the Future of Japan-Russia Ties
articles.full_text:
The Kuril Islands dispute is not just a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan but reflects the larger complexity of geopolitical dynamics in the Indo-Pacific Region.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visiting the Kurilsk Central District Hospital on Iturup Island, Aug. 13, 2026.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the Kuril Islands on August 12. He became the second Russian leader to visit the islands, after President Dmitry Medvedev’s landmark trip in 2010. More recently, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited the islands in 2021. 
Putin’s recent visit prompted a protest from Japan, with Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae calling the visit an offense to the sentiments of the Japanese people and unacceptable. 
The islands have been the subject of an ongoing territorial dispute between Japan and Russia, both historically and under international law, for over 80 years. Russia calls the islands the Kuril Islands, and Japan calls them the Northern Territories; the volcanic islands lie at the heart of a territorial feud that has prevented the two countries from formally ending World War II, despite signing a joint declaration for restoring diplomatic relations in 1956. 
Putin’s recent visit has made it even harder to restore relations between the countries. 
There are 56 islands in the 1,300-kilometer (810-mile) archipelago that stretches from Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula to Hokkaido, separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean. Japan claims four of the islands. These include Iturup (Etorofu in Japanese), Kunashir (Kunashiri), Shikotan, and Habomai, the southernmost islands and closest to Japan, just off the coast of Hokkaido. While Russia administers the islands as part of the Sakhalin region, Japan considers the four they claim as part of Hokkaido prefecture and argues that they are “illegally occupied” by Russia.
In 1855, in the first treaty between tsarist Russia and Japan, the frontier between the two countries was drawn just north of the four islands closest to Japan. Twenty years later, a new treaty handed the entire chain to Japan, in exchange for Russia gaining full control of the island of Sakhalin. Japan seized back control of the southern half of Sakhalin during its crushing victory in the 1905 Russo-Japanese War. 
In August 1945, as the Soviet Union entered the war with Japan just after the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, the Kuril Islands emerged as a flashpoint. Soviet troops completed their takeover of the islands after Japan surrendered. The Soviet capture of the islands has prevented Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal treaty to end the war, despite repeated attempts over the past 80 years to reach agreement. 
In 1956, both Moscow and Tokyo signed a joint declaration that ended their state of war and restored diplomatic relations – though it was not a formal treaty ending the war. As part of the declaration, the Soviet side agreed to transfer Shikotan and the Habomai Islands to Japan. Negotiations continued after the Cold War, producing results such as the 1993 Tokyo Declaration and 2001 Irkutsk Statement, the latter of which reaffirmed the 1956 declaration as the baseline legal foundation for peace talks. 
Under Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, talks intensified in 2018, including the drafting of a peace treaty based on the 1956 declaration. However, the process collapsed with the start of the Ukraine war in 2022, when Russia suspended peace-treaty negotiations due to Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow.
The Kuril Islands are far more than a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan; they are a lesser-known strategic fault line in the evolving Indo-Pacific order. Home to around 20,000 people across the chain, the islands are economically and strategically valuable because they are rich in fish stocks and contain deposits of minerals and rare metals, including rhenium, which is used in the production of supersonic aircraft. 
For Russia, however, the islands’ greatest value is military. Bases and missile systems on the Kurils help secure Moscow’s Pacific Fleet and reinforce the Sea of Okhotsk as a nuclear bastion. Control of the islands gives Russia year-round access to the Pacific Ocean for its Pacific Fleet, based in Vladivostok, since the strait between Kunashir and Iturup does not freeze in winter. They are also a launchpad for maritime outreach through the Northern Sea Route.
While Russian and Chinese warships recently conducted Joint Sea 2026, an annual bilateral naval exercise, through waters around the Kuril chain, Russian naval forces have also conducted exercises in the Far East. 
By tightening its grip on the islands, Moscow is not merely defending territory but also challenging the existing regional balance. This complicates the strategic calculations of the U.S.-led Indo-Pacific alliance, including Japan’s Indo-Pacific outlook, adding another layer of complexity to the evolving region.
For Japan, the dispute is increasingly connected to the wider security challenge posed by a possible Taiwan contingency. Russian military activity in the region could complicate Japan’s ability to focus exclusively on threats closer to Taiwan and the East China Sea. 
The implications extend well beyond Russia and Japan. Joint Chinese-Russian naval activity around the Kurils signal growing strategic convergence between Moscow and Beijing. China’s silence and neutral stance on Japan’s territorial claim further strengthens Russia’s position while placing additional pressure on Tokyo. 
The timing of Putin’s visit to Iturup Island was notable. It came two days before Japan marked 81 years since its surrender ended ​World War II. It also came a day after North Korea fired a missile into the Sea of Japan (East Sea) and just days before major South Korea-U.S. military exercises, Ulchi Freedom Shield, were scheduled to begin. The timing suggests a coordinated display of military and geopolitical pressure around Japan, highlighting Japan’s increasingly difficult security environment.
The Kuril Islands dispute is not just a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan but reflects the larger complexity of geopolitical dynamics in the Indo-Pacific Region.
The possibility of peace between Japan and Russia seems bleak at this juncture, after the closing of another window of opportunity for the two countries to engage in a beneficial tradeoff between Russian energy and Japanese technology and investments. The dispute may remain a long-term strategic flashpoint, limiting economic cooperation while intensifying wider geopolitical competition in the Indo-Pacific. This may eventually lead Japan to harden its security posture and deepen its alignment with the U.S. and other Indo-Pacific partners, further reducing prospects for any Japan-Russia rapprochement.

Putin’s recent visit has made it even harder to restore relations between the countries. 
There are 56 islands in the 1,300-kilometer (810-mile) archipelago that stretches from Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula to Hokkaido, separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean. Japan claims four of the islands. These include Iturup (Etorofu in Japanese), Kunashir (Kunashiri), Shikotan, and Habomai, the southernmost islands and closest to Japan, just off the coast of Hokkaido. While Russia administers the islands as part of the Sakhalin region, Japan considers the four they claim as part of Hokkaido prefecture and argues that they are “illegally occupied” by Russia.
In 1855, in the first treaty between tsarist Russia and Japan, the frontier between the two countries was drawn just north of the four islands closest to Japan. Twenty years later, a new treaty handed the entire chain to Japan, in exchange for Russia gaining full control of the island of Sakhalin. Japan seized back control of the southern half of Sakhalin during its crushing victory in the 1905 Russo-Japanese War. 
In August 1945, as the Soviet Union entered the war with Japan just after the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, the Kuril Islands emerged as a flashpoint. Soviet troops completed their takeover of the islands after Japan surrendered. The Soviet capture of the islands has prevented Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal treaty to end the war, despite repeated attempts over the past 80 years to reach agreement. 
In 1956, both Moscow and Tokyo signed a joint declaration that ended their state of war and restored diplomatic relations – though it was not a formal treaty ending the war. As part of the declaration, the Soviet side agreed to transfer Shikotan and the Habomai Islands to Japan. Negotiations continued after the Cold War, producing results such as the 1993 Tokyo Declaration and 2001 Irkutsk Statement, the latter of which reaffirmed the 1956 declaration as the baseline legal foundation for peace talks. 
Under Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, talks intensified in 2018, including the drafting of a peace treaty based on the 1956 declaration. However, the process collapsed with the start of the Ukraine war in 2022, when Russia suspended peace-treaty negotiations due to Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow.
The Kuril Islands are far more than a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan; they are a lesser-known strategic fault line in the evolving Indo-Pacific order. Home to around 20,000 people across the chain, the islands are economically and strategically valuable because they are rich in fish stocks and contain deposits of minerals and rare metals, including rhenium, which is used in the production of supersonic aircraft.
articles.summary: The Kuril Islands dispute is not just a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan but reflects the larger complexity of geopolitical dynamics in the Indo-Pacific Region.

articles.title: Principled Caution: Navigating AI in Asian Newsrooms
articles.full_text:
In many Asian countries, letting an AI-generated error slip through could mean not only reputational harm but legal and political persecution
Across Asia, public interest media are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to optimize under-resourced newsrooms. However, these outlets face a high-stakes reality: publishing AI-generated errors, factual inaccuracies, or “AI slop” risks undermining the public trust and credibility central to their legitimacy. At the same time, these media are also aware that they are operating in authoritarian contexts where AI-induced mistakes can lead to legal and political persecution.
Hence, independent outlets in the Asia-Pacific – the media that produce journalism essential to democratic accountability – exercise “principled caution” when deploying AI. They exercise this caution not just because of a desire to maintain their reputation for accuracy. They also do so because there is a real risk of forced state closure, the freezing of assets, or the imprisonment of staff. 
This is the core finding of Asia Centre’s latest report, “Principled caution: How AI is used in public-interest media in Asia,” published in partnership with DW Akademie and supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Evaluating media ecosystems across eight Asian countries – Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Myanmar, Pakistan, and Uzbekistan – the study reveals how journalists are managing AI adoption. Rather than blind adoption, Asia’s independent public interest media are approaching AI through a careful and highly selective strategy. In structurally precarious environments where reporting errors can invite censorship, legal action, or operational shutdown, outlets consistently prioritize human editorial oversight over full-scale automation.  
The report identifies several key findings:
First, AI usage in newsrooms remains assistive rather than transformative. Outlets primarily use generative AI tools at the preliminary and final stages of editorial workflows, for tasks such as ideation, document summarization, social media adaptation, and headline polishing. The central stages of journalistic work – including original field reporting, investigative narrative drafting, and editorial judgment – remain strictly human-driven.
Second, severe language constraints mean that major global Large Language Models underperform in low-resource Asian languages, including Bahasa Indonesia, Bangla, Burmese, Chittagonian, Dzongkha, Farsi, Jingpo, Khmer, Pashto, and Urdu. These platforms frequently mistranslate context-sensitive terms, flatten cultural nuances, and generate wrong outputs. While translation is the most widely adopted AI task, outputs require labor-intensive human correction.
Third, exiled media from countries like Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Pakistan face distinct operational threats including digital surveillance, internet blackouts, cross-border security risks, and severe financial instability. These pressures leave little mental or institutional bandwidth to experiment with new technologies. Yet, securely tailored automated tools for transcription, translation, and media-monitoring offer an unrealized opportunity to engage diaspora networks and report on repressed homelands without compromising journalists’ digital safety.
Fourth, a sharp institutional deficit persists across newsrooms. Over 60 percent of surveyed newsrooms report that AI adoption occurs via ad-hoc, individual staff experimentation rather than cohesive organizational strategies. Structural gaps, such as the absence of formal editorial guidelines, missing data protection protocols, and a heavy reliance on Big Tech platforms, leave independent media vulnerable to algorithmic bias, privacy violations, copyright risks, and state surveillance.
Fifth, restrictive political and legal environments across Asia impede responsible AI adoption. While state authorities deploy automated systems for online monitoring, surveillance, and synthetic media campaigns, regulatory ambiguity is routinely weaponized to clamp down on media freedoms. Public interest newsrooms face a stark structural asymmetry; political actors deploy AI at scale to amplify state narratives and disinformation, while underfunded independent outlets lack affordable verification tools to counter these attacks effectively. 
Looking ahead, AI integration in Asian newsrooms cannot rely solely on off-the-shelf tools built by Western tech monopolies. Long-term media sustainability requires localized AI infrastructure, enforceable newsroom governance frameworks, and open-source language models tailored to the region’s complex political and linguistic contexts. Without this shift toward technological sovereignty, regional media risk becoming mere data points for foreign algorithmic models that operate without local democratic stakes. We must move beyond being passive consumers of black-box solutions and start architecting a digital future that respects our region’s unique socio-political boundaries.
To achieve this, international donors and media development actors must pivot away from short-term, surface-level training sessions. Instead, capital must be redirected toward regional and local entities to lead core technological infrastructure, secure data storage systems, and create collaborative AI hubs specifically designed to serve independent and exiled media. This requires reimagining “capacity building” as the construction of resilient, shared digital architectures that treat cybersecurity as a foundational reporting tool. By financing regional and local based collective defense, we can turn isolated public interest newsrooms into fortified digital outposts capable of weathering persistent state-sponsored surveillance.
Ultimately, the future of journalism in Asia will not be determined by the speed of algorithmic tools, but by whether newsrooms can harness AI without compromising the trust, accuracy, and independence that underpin public interest reporting. In an era of synthetic media floods, human-centric rigor is not a hurdle to innovation – it is our ultimate competitive advantage. Those who prioritize ethical safeguards now will be the only ones to retain audience loyalty when the inevitable global backlash against AI-generated misinformation arrives.
This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Principled caution: How AI is used in public-interest media in Asia”. Download the full report here. For more information about the Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org.

articles.title: What Does Japan Think of the Sudden Cut to South Korea-US Joint Drills?
articles.full_text:
Although Japanese leaders have been publicly quiet, this incident highlights several points of concern that have existed since the second Trump administration.
Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) airmen assigned to the 3rd Air Wing run to secure the perimeter of an emergency scene during an aircraft mass casualty exercise at Misawa Air Base, Japan, Aug. 26, 2026.
On August 16, U.S. President Donald Trump scaled back military drills with South Korea. In a social media post, he cited three different explanations for the move: the cost of the exercises to the United States, his supposedly friendly relations with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and his displeasure over perceived lack of South Korean support for the U.S. war effort against Iran. 
After Trump’s intervention, the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, which started on August 17, only ran through August 21 instead of the originally scheduled August 27. In practice, the first phase of the exercise – focused on defense – was preserved while the second phase – focused on counterattack – was canceled. In addition, live-training exercises were replaced with simulations. 
According to the South Korean new agency Yonhap, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told the legislature that “Neither our government nor U.S. officials knew what President Trump wrote on his Truth Social account.” In a meeting with the National Assembly Committee on Foreign Affairs and Unification, Cho said, “We were not notified in advance.”
On August 24, the United States canceled the biennial Ssangyong drills, a large joint amphibious landing exercise, scheduled for September. This time, the justification was constraints on force availability caused by the Iran war. This announcement was not as abrupt, as the U.S. Marine Corps had officially notified Seoul back in June that its force availability would likely be constrained. 
On August 28, the United States, South Korea, and Japan announced that they will conduct the annual Freedom Edge drills, joint military drills to test readiness against North Korea’s missiles and nuclear weapons threat, from September 9 to 11. 
What is Japan’s perspective on the latest developments in the South Korea-U.S. alliance? 
Japan’s initial reaction has been muted. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro responded to the announcement by saying: “As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States, and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region.” The statement, however, did not actually criticize the U.S. decision to scale back joint exercises.
Although Japanese leaders have been publicly quiet, this incident highlights several points of concern that have existed since the second Trump administration.  
First, it could indicate a more aggressive move by Washington to resume talks with North Korea. Japan would always have been wary of a North Korea-U.S. deal that advanced U.S. security while sidelining Japanese concerns. For example, a hypothetical deal could cut back on Pyongyang’s long-range missiles, which can reach the United States, but do nothing to reduce its stockpile of short-range missiles, which can reach Japan. The threat to Japan remains persistent, as North Korea fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles on August 20; this was the third ballistic missile test in August. 
There is also a question of whether the United States will maintain denuclearization as a policy objective, and what Japan will do vis-à-vis North Korea if the United States abandons it. Conservative Japanese leaders also have a vested political interest in the return of abductees, an issue that might get ignored in a North Korea-U.S. deal. 
Japanese analysts worry about a more emboldened North Korea, though at the same time they doubt the likelihood of a U.S. overture to Pyongyang succeeding. But experts have failed to predict many aspects of this administration’s foreign policy. 
U.S. overtures to North Korea, reciprocated or not, will likely be reflected in the three strategy documents currently being revised in Tokyo: the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Defense Buildup Program. Japan intends to finish updating these documents by the end of the year. Tokyo could also, much more quietly, consider nuclear weapons for itself if questions about the credibility of the U.S. nuclear deterrent being to mount. 
Another worrying aspect of Trump’s social media post is the signal that the United States is prepared to more explicitly make assistance in the Iran War a condition of continued support. Certainly, there are different dynamics between the South Korea-U.S. alliance and that between Japan and the United States. For one, Japan has long relied on its constitutional and legal framework to avoid entanglement in U.S. wars. However, the Trump administration may be less sympathetic to such justifications. If they cannot force Japan to support U.S. military operations in the Strait of Hormuz due to Japan’s constraints, Washington may demand concessions from Japan in other areas, such as reduced joint exercises or increased host nation support. 
This administration has shown a tendency to link security and economic issues in a way that previous administrations usually did not (i.e., reducing the benefit of the training exercise to its financial costs). The timing is particularly worrying for Japan as Tokyo begins negotiations with Washington over host nation support. A sudden demand for a large increase is certainly possible. 
Trump’s decision – announced on the same day Ulchi Freedom Shield began – makes it clear that U.S. military exercises can be scaled down on a moment’s notice. Japan has its own exercises with the United States, Keen Sword, in October. Though it is expected to be smaller than the 2024 iteration due to U.S. deployments in the Iran war, it could be scaled back even farther. Trump could use the same three-fold justification he used against South Korea to cancel or scale down these exercises. 
In a related concern, Trump’s rationale for the decision showed his susceptibility to accepting autocrats’ talking points. Trump appears to have bought Kim’s argument that the training exercises are aggressive, while the U.S. and South Korean governments have long maintained that these exercises are defensive. It’s odd, to say the least, to see a U.S. president describing actions by the South Korea-U.S. alliance as “totally inappropriate and hostile” and North Korea as “unthreatening and respectful.”
Finally, there is real concern about what it would mean for U.S military readiness on the Korean Peninsula and in the Indo-Pacific more broadly if training exercises become scaled back or more erratic.
Alliance readiness is a key concern. While North Korean soldiers are returning to the peninsula after having real world battle experience in the Russia-Ukraine war, the best that the U.S. and South Korean soldiers can do to prepare is live trainings. Yet these live trainings are being replaced by simulations at the same time the enemy is “training” by engaging in real combat. 
A U.S. Department of Defense official said in a statement that “These adjustments preserve essential readiness and training objectives,” and “There will be no degradation to U.S. training objectives.” But saying the sky is pink does not make it so.

articles.title: What a Chongqing Fandom Clash Reveals About China’s Gender Divide
articles.full_text:
Male “anti-fan” livestreamers invaded a boy-band training event — and targeted the largely female fan base.
Graffiti near the Time Fengjun headquarters after the violent protests reads: “Please let girls be themselves.”
Waving Chinese national flags and singing the military anthem are sights more commonly associated with state-sanctioned patriotic rallies. Yet on the night of August 18 along Chongqing’s Nanbin Road, young men used these patriotic symbols while marching against a seemingly bizarre enemy: teenage idol trainees of a boy-band talent agency and their female fans.
What began as a localized dispute outside the headquarters of Shidai Fengjun (also known as “Time Fengjun,” or TF Entertainment), an agency that helped pioneer China’s idol-trainee industry, rapidly escalated into a prolonged public disturbance. For days, the area around the agency saw escalating street violence, culminating in a heavy police presence and roadblocks. 
The confrontation offered a glimpse into a broader dynamic in contemporary China: how online male grievances can spill into the streets, how nationalist symbols can be mobilized in gender conflicts, and how authorities struggle to contain the resulting unrest.
The trouble began on August 15, when groups of male short-video livestreamers and “anti-fans” (黑粉) repeatedly gathered outside Time Fengjun’s office building. Many appeared to be seeking online traffic and attention. They burned and tore down fan posters, blocked company vans, and confronted the company’s young trainees, some reportedly as young as 11. They livestreamed the confrontations while shouting “jiahao” (嘉豪), a derogatory internet term mocking young men who try too hard to appear “cool.” The chant appeared intended as a deliberate provocation. 
The incident took on a broader gender dimension after a viral video clip circulated on August 17. The footage captured a female fan throwing a small object (variously reported as a power bank or water bottle) at a male provocateur, who responded by splashing water at her and appeared to move toward her aggressively. When police on site immediately detained the male provocateur but did not detain the female fan, online male communities erupted in fury. 
Accusing police of giving women preferential treatment, commenters began using terms such as “maternal law enforcement” (秉母执法, bingmu zhifa), a pun on binggong zhifa (秉公执法, “impartial law enforcement”), and “Chongqing maternal public security” to portray local authorities as biased in favor of female fans.
Driven by this digital rage, crowds of young men marched down Nanbin Road on August 18, demanding the release of the detained men. They wrapped their grievances in the language of patriotism, waving Chinese national flags and singing the national anthem and the military anthem “Strong Army Song” (《强军战歌》) as they marched. 
Patriotic rhetoric gave the confrontation a broader political frame. Some protesters portrayed the predominantly female fan community as a symbol of what they saw as a feminized and “decadent” youth culture, casting their confrontation with the fans as a fight to “realize justice.”
As the marchers gathered around the building, the confrontation turned physical. Livestreamers chased, kicked, and assaulted female fans. Videos circulating online showed ordinary women and girls caught in the confrontation. In some footage, female fans were surrounded, cornered, shoved, kicked, or splashed with liquid. Chinese-language media also reported that a mother and daughter were among those assaulted, although their relationship is difficult to independently verify from the footage. 
In response, Time Fengjun suspended its trainees’ offline sessions on August 18, but faced intense criticism from female fans for failing to protect them and remaining silent about the violence.
As the physical crowds swelled, the conflict spilled back online into more serious digital harassment. Online vigilantes doxed female fans on site, leaking their personal identities. The harassers used AI tools to splice the victims’ faces onto non-consensual pornographic images, which were then printed on flyers advertising prostitution and distributed both online and in person.
Facing several days of increasingly visible unrest, local authorities moved to contain the confrontation. Physically, police blocked roads and used municipal buses to disperse and evict the male protesters. Online, videos about the incident, and posts and searches containing terms such as “bingmu zhifa” appeared to face censorship on major Chinese social-media platforms.
On August 20, the Chongqing Public Security Bureau released a brief statement. It downplayed the gender-targeted physical and digital violence, dryly framing the multi-day unrest as a minor “fandom dispute” involving “water-throwing and chasing.” It offered “legal education” to participants and called for “civilized fan activities.”
By reducing the confrontation to a fandom dispute, authorities restored temporary order while leaving the gender grievances that fueled the conflict largely unaddressed. The Chongqing confrontation illustrated how online male grievance can move rapidly from digital spaces into the physical world, especially when it becomes entangled with broader anxieties over gender and masculinity. 
Meanwhile, censorship on Chinese social media platforms makes it increasingly difficult to document and verify such incidents domestically, leaving overseas platforms such as X and Threads as important sources of evidence and further widening the information gap between China and the outside world.

articles.title: Militant Buildup in Areas Critical to China’s Economic Interests in Pakistan
articles.full_text:
The TTP has stepped up its presence along the Karakoram Highway, even as Pakistan and China discuss $1.8 billion in financing to realign its Thakot-Raikot section.
Aerial view of the Karakoram Highway in Pakistan as seen in 2021.
With the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), a critical node of the Belt and Road Initiative in Pakistan, entering its second phase, insurgent and terrorist networks in Pakistan are strategically positioning themselves in areas critical to CPEC’s future.
CPEC connects China’s western Xinjiang province with the Arabian Sea. It enters Pakistan from the northern Gilgit-Baltistan area and culminates at Gwadar Port in Balochistan province.
While the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) is gradually increasing its footprint in Pakistan’s northern belt, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has ramped up attacks in Balochistan, multiplying China’s security challenges.
The deteriorating security situation in southwestern Balochistan and northern Pakistan is expected to disrupt future CPEC projects and China-Pakistan economic cooperation, thereby weakening Pakistan’s economy. The timing of militant buildup in these areas is vital; it is happening against the backdrop of intense U.S.-China competition over critical minerals in Balochistan.

Then, in April 2026, TTP claimed responsibility for attacking police in Gilgit Baltistan’s Chilas area.
Concurrently, TTP’s network has re-emerged in Malakand Division, which abuts Gilgit Baltistan. On August 2, TTP claimed a suicide attack outside a police station in Swat, which killed 17 people and wounded dozens of others. Monitoring Committee on Al-Qaeda and ISIL report indicates reconcentration of the East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM)’s fighters in northern Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province, which shares a border with Gilgit Baltistan. articles.title: One Nation’s Dual Assault on Australia’s Structural Realities
articles.full_text:
With a below replacement-level birth rate and a booming elder population, One Nation’s anti-immigration stance, combined with its critique of superannuation, is a toxic combo.
A major structural issue facing most Western and East Asian countries at present is their below replacement-level birth rates. This has the potential to create an unfavorable dependency ratio – the problem of aging societies with a large cohort of retirees, but not enough workers to pay for pensions, healthcare, and other essential services. 
Yet simultaneously, many Western countries are experiencing an insurgence of populist, and often extremist, parties hostile to the one mechanism available to alleviate this problem: immigration. In Australia, this year has seen the rise of One Nation – previously a small fringe anti-immigrant party – now consistently polling in the mid-high 20 percent range. One Nation often matches the governing Labor Party’s poll numbers, and is polling far ahead of Australia’s other traditional major political force, the permanent coalition between the Liberal and National parties. 
One Nation’s reason for existence is to undermine Australia’s migration program – which it sees as a threat to their idea of the Australian nation. Yet as the party has ascended in the polls it has needed to branch out into other populist causes and conspiratorial theories to promote. One issue the party has landed on is Australia’s retirement savings scheme – known as superannuation. 
Australia’s superannuation scheme was made compulsory in its modern form by the Keating government in 1992, requiring employers to contribute a portion of workers’ wages into privately managed retirement funds. The contribution rate has gradually risen to 12 percent – paid on top of wages – and has created one of the world’s largest pools of retirement savings. It is accessible at 60 years old. The basic idea is simple: Australians build up their own nest egg during their working lives, reducing their reliance on the government-funded Age Pension in retirement. Superannuation is ranked one of the world’s leading retirement schemes.  
However, there’s always been a strain of suspicion toward superannuation within the Liberal Party. This stems in part from politics – the scheme was introduced by the Labor Party, after all – and in part from the perception of the scheme as paternalistic and undermining the personal responsibility to save for yourself. 
But within a consumerist culture, turbo-charged by the ease of online shopping and the relentless product promotion of online influencers, it is arguable that the scheme has saved a great many Australians from difficult retirements. Personal responsibility is important, but there also needs to be a recognition that we are an easily tempted species and sometimes we need some guardrails for our own good. 
One Nation’s opposition to superannuation appeals directly to these critiques. As a populist party, it simply says: “You can have more money in your pocket today and the government is keeping it from you.” It may appeal to those suffering current cost of living pressures and who are distrustful of government initiatives, but it plays a dangerous game with Australia’s structural realities. Alongside the party’s suspicion of immigration, is a dual assault on the future sustainability of the Australian state. 
Given Australia’s birth rate of 1.48 births per woman, the Treasury estimates that a migration intake of at least 235,000 people a year is required to off-set the worst effects of an aging society. This, of course, isn’t perfect, as the median age of a migrant to Australia is 37. This is around 20 less years paying tax than someone who enters the workforce in their mid-to-late teens. But, given the realities of low birth rates, it is the best solution available.  
Despite some internal confusion, the figure One Nation has consistently cited as their policy is 130,000 people per year – although they channel forces that even find this number unacceptably high. This combination with a populace who had greater access to their retirement savings prior to retirement would create an enormous government pension outlay without the tax base to cover it. 
Rather than seek ways to off-set a poor dependency ratio, One Nation’s policies are now trying to accelerate it. This is, of course, the nature of the party. Populist parties don’t have a long-term comprehension of the economic sustainability of the country. They fixate on immediate grievances and emotional responses. The implications and consequences of their ideas are not well thought out. 
This should present an opportunity for the Liberal Party to regain the ground they’ve lost to One Nation this year. Although there are elements within the party likewise suspicious of superannuation, the Liberals’ traditional selling point has been responsible economic stewardship of the country. The problem the party faces, however, is that administrative sobriety isn’t very attractive at the moment. The people want more and they want it now, even if it may lead to them having far less as they age.

articles.title: Tokayev Sets Agenda for Kazakhstan as New Parliament Gets to Work
articles.full_text:
The change in form promised by Kazakhstan’s new parliament does not appear to be matched by a change in its function.
Kazakhstan’s new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai, gathered for its first session today. On August 23 the all-but-ordained Adilet party triumphed over an array of officially sanctioned opposition parties, winning a thumping 71 percent of the vote in the first election after Kazakhstan’s March constitutional revamp.
According to the Central Electoral Commission, which registered new legislators in an official ceremony on August 27, Adilet will have 110 deputies of a possible 145 sitting in the new body, likely led by presidential advisor-turned-party leader Aibek Dadebay. 
As for its legislative agenda, all signs indicate that the Kurultai will largely pick up where the old parliament left off. Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev spent the last week plotting a roadmap for the incoming Kurultai, and his to-do list is grounded in long-standing governmental priorities. 
On August 27, for example, citing the example of “several well-developed countries,” Tokayev said he planned to ask Kurultai deputies to consider banning social media for children under the age of 16, in what will essentially be a continuation of a bill submitted to parliament in June, according to local independent media outlet Vlast.kz. 
In a similar vein, speaking at an educators’ conference on August 26, Tokayev called on the government to take more urgent measures to implement his May presidential decree on the introduction of artificial intelligence into the national education system. The directive came as part of the country’s Year of Artificial Intelligence program, itself a continuation of the broader strategy on AI launched in 2025 following the creation of the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. 
Amid these more conventional proposals, Tokayev’s most interesting comments arguably came during  an appearance at a polling station on August 23 — and not only because he rebuked his compatriots for hugging and kissing in contravention of the country’s “time-honored traditions,” and called on Kazakhstani men to instead shake hands “firmly,” not like a “warm cutlet or a twig.” 
Speaking after casting his ballot, Tokayev also suggested that Kazakhstan needed to be “turned into a major building site,” and proposed transferring significant amounts of money from the National Fund to spur this drive for development, a policy hastily confirmed by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin at a briefing on August 25. 
According to Zhumangarin, Kazakhstan’s government is set to withdraw nearly 12 trillion tenge ($26.2 billion) from the National Fund, the country’s sovereign wealth fund, despite pledging last summer to scale down transfers through 2028 to reduce the national budget’s dependence on oil revenues. (Kazakhstan’s National Fund is largely financed by revenues generated from the country’s oil and other extractive industries, with a portion of these revenues saved and invested for future generations.)
This too, however, equates to picking up where previous governments left off. As Kazakhstani political scientist Daniyar Ashimbayev wrote, “the National Fund has for years been actively misappropriated for unclear purposes,” with the state dipping into the reserve to inject money into the economy, “without concerning itself with the wisdom of such spending.” 
What this all means is that the change in form promised by Kazakhstan’s new parliament does not appear to be matched by a change in its function. The Kurultai may have a number of new politicians taking their seats today, but the policies, practices, and priorities shaping the country’s politics remain largely unchanged.
